passages.title: How to Document High-Value Contents
passages.heading: What makes an item high-value for documentation purposes?
passages.text: Not a dollar threshold — whether small differences in identity change the replacement cost materially. Where brand, model, configuration, edition or condition move the price, the identification has to carry that detail. “Camera — $2,000” could be an entry-level mirrorless body, a professional full-frame body, a modest body with an expensive lens, or a discontinued specialty model. Those are four different claims, and the schedule cannot tell a reviewer which one it is.

passages.title: How to Document High-Value Contents
passages.heading: Where the detail earns its keep
passages.text: Configuration that materially changes replacement cost Category What has to be captured Camera systems Body and lens are often separate lines, not one item Computers Processor, memory, storage and screen size Power tools Battery platform and kit configuration, which can double a price Musical instruments Model, finish, pickups, hardware, whether the case is included Designer goods Material, size, collection and edition Watches Reference number, movement, bracelet and box or papers Premium appliances Capacity, fuel type and finish A high-value item reduced to its category has lost precisely the information that would have justified its value.

passages.title: How to Document High-Value Contents
passages.heading: What to photograph
passages.text: One frame establishes the property existed. What prices it is the second and third: the manufacturer mark, the model or serial plate, the feature that sets the tier, and the damage. All of those describe one item and belong on one line. Receipts, purchase histories and warranty records are worth digging out before the list is built, not after a figure is questioned. On expensive property they frequently settle the configuration question that photographs alone cannot.

passages.title: How to Document High-Value Contents
passages.heading: Use the market the item actually trades in
passages.text: The source should match the property Item Where a defensible figure comes from Current premium television Ordinary retail — the same model is on sale now Professional camera body Authorised dealer or major retailer Discontinued luxury handbag Specialist resale, where that item actually trades Collectible Collector marketplace, judged on edition and condition Vintage instrument Specialist dealer or the secondary market Where retail can price the item, it should. Where it genuinely cannot, Kevin prices from the resale market instead, used raw and labelled as resale so a used-market figure is never read as a new-replacement one.

passages.title: How to Document High-Value Contents
passages.heading: High value does not mean unpriced — or undepreciated
passages.text: There is no dollar threshold in Kevin that sends a line for approval. If the evidence supports a price, the item is priced whatever the amount; a $10,000 sofa prices like any other sofa. What is never auto-priced is a set of appraisal classes — jewelry, firearms, fine arts, furs, fine china and graded trading cards. Those arrive unpriced by design, because a number produced without an appraisal on that property is worse than a blank. Separately, and it is a different list, some classes carry a policy sub-limit and are flagged amber on the worksheet: fine jewelry, firearms, fine arts, furs and collectible coins. That cue flags; it never blocks. Depreciation still applies on its own terms. High value is not a reason to skip it, and the class rather than the price decides the useful life.

passages.title: How to Document High-Value Contents
passages.heading: Spend review where the money is
passages.text: The point of automating the repetitive part of a claim is to buy attention for the lines that deserve it. On a large inventory those are the ambiguous identifications, the unusual products, the discontinued property, the condition-sensitive markets — and anything whose price sits a long way from its neighbours for no visible reason. The worksheet filters to high-value lines so you can work them as a group, which is a view, not a gate.

passages.title: How to Document High-Value Contents
passages.heading: Common questions
passages.text: Should high-value items be listed separately? Nearly always. The moment an item’s value turns on brand, model, configuration or condition, grouping it with similar-looking property throws away the detail that justifies the number. Is one photo enough for a high-value item? Rarely. One frame establishes that the property existed; a second of the model plate establishes which product it was, and that is what the price is argued from. On expensive property the marginal photograph is the cheapest evidence you will ever collect. Should a generic replacement be used if the exact item is unavailable? Only if it genuinely matches on the characteristics that gave the original its value. High-value property is exactly where a loose like-kind substitution is most visible and most costly — a tier drop on a $4,000 item is a bigger error than the whole value of most lines on the claim. Does a high price make something high-value for documentation purposes? Not quite. The real test is whether small differences in identity change the replacement cost materially. A $900 appliance where the model barely moves the price needs less identification than a $900 handbag where the line and the year move it a great deal. Does Kevin refuse to price expensive items? No. If the evidence supports a price, the item is priced regardless of the amount — there is no dollar threshold that sends a line for approval. What is never auto-priced is a set of appraisal classes: jewelry, firearms, fine arts, furs, fine china and graded trading cards reach you unpriced by design. What is the amber flag on some rows? A coverage-cap cue, not a problem with the line. It marks classes that typically carry a policy sub-limit — fine jewelry, firearms, fine arts, furs and collectible coins. It flags, never blocks, and it is a different set from the appraisal classes: fine china and graded cards are never auto-priced but carry no sub-limit.

passages.title: How to Price Collectibles in Contents Claims
passages.heading: How is a collectible valued on a contents claim?
passages.text: By identifying the exact item — edition, release, condition, completeness — and then finding what a genuinely comparable example trades for, usually in a specialist or resale market rather than ordinary retail. Ordinary replacement-cost research assumes a current product stands in for the damaged one. For a collectible that assumption frequently fails: there may be no current product, and two examples that photograph identically can be worth very different amounts.

passages.title: How to Price Collectibles in Contents Claims
passages.heading: Identify before pricing — further than usual
passages.text: Detail that changes the value, not just the description Attribute Why it moves the figure Edition or release A reissue and a first release are different markets Year and production run Scarcity is usually a function of both Condition or grade Often the single largest factor in the price Packaging Sealed, boxed or loose can be separate markets Completeness Missing inserts or accessories change the comparable Authentication Graded or certified examples trade against each other Markings Serial, issue number or mint mark can decide the edition A vague description does not produce a vague price here — it produces a confident price for a different item.

passages.title: How to Price Collectibles in Contents Claims
passages.heading: Five listings, five different items
passages.text: Suppose a search returns five results: one sealed, one opened but complete, one missing accessories, one damaged, and one a different edition. Averaging them produces a number, and the number means nothing, because the five are not comparables for each other. This is why Kevin prices a line from one listing rather than a blend of several , with the Source Link pointing at it. A blended figure hides exactly the question a collectible line needs answered: which example is this price for?

passages.title: How to Price Collectibles in Contents Claims
passages.heading: Asking prices, and what Kevin holds
passages.text: An active listing shows what a seller is asking. A completed sale shows what somebody paid. In thin or volatile collectible markets the second is often the better evidence of how the market actually behaves, and an adjuster researching one unusual item by hand is right to look for it. Kevin prices from active listings. Every comp it surfaces is a current offer, so the figures are asking prices on listings that exist now, never records of past transactions. On a collectible where completed sales are the stronger evidence, that is a line worth pricing yourself and attaching your own source to — which the worksheet supports on any row.

passages.title: How to Price Collectibles in Contents Claims
passages.heading: Sets, lots and single pieces
passages.text: Collectibles are sold as individual pieces, sets, lots, complete series and partial series, and the same search will return all of them. A set price must not value one piece, and a single piece must not value a series. On quantity-heavy collections this is the error that compounds fastest.

passages.title: How to Price Collectibles in Contents Claims
passages.heading: What Kevin will not price automatically
passages.text: Some collectible property never reaches the pricing engine at all. Graded trading cards and fine china are appraisal classes , alongside jewelry, firearms, fine arts and furs — they arrive unpriced, with an editable field, because a number produced without an appraisal on that property is worse than a blank. Separately, and this is a different list, some classes carry a policy sub-limit and are flagged amber on the worksheet: fine jewelry, firearms, fine arts, furs and collectible coins . The two sets deliberately do not match — graded cards are never auto-priced but carry no sub-limit, and the amber cue flags coverage, not a problem with the line.

passages.title: How to Price Collectibles in Contents Claims
passages.heading: Record why the comparable is the comparable
passages.text: The further a comparable sits from the exact item, the more the reasoning carries the line. A collectible line should let a reviewer see what the item was, which edition and condition were documented, what source was used and why that example is relevant — because none of it is obvious from an ordinary retail search.

passages.title: How to Price Collectibles in Contents Claims
passages.heading: Common questions
passages.text: Should collectibles be priced from eBay? Often that is the only market where the item actually trades, so yes — with more scrutiny than a retail listing needs. The comparable has to match on item, edition, condition and completeness, any one of which can move the value further than the category does. Are asking prices reliable? They are evidence, not a verdict. An active listing shows what one seller wants; in a thin collectible market the spread between asking prices can be enormous, and the high end is often a different edition, a sealed example, or somebody not really expecting to sell. Does Kevin price from completed sales? No. Every comp Kevin surfaces is a current offer, retail and resale alike, so the figures are asking prices on listings that exist now rather than records of past transactions. For a collectible where completed sales are the better evidence, that is a line worth pricing yourself and attaching your own source to. Should collectibles be depreciated like ordinary household goods? Not necessarily, and class assignment is what decides it. Several collectible categories carry materially longer useful lives than short-life household goods, and some are appraisal classes that are never automatically priced at all. Does packaging affect collectible value? For some categories it dominates it. A sealed example and the same item opened can be different markets, and completeness — inserts, accessories, certificates — moves the figure again. Where that is true, the inventory should say which one the insured owned. Can Kevin price rare items? It can research the resale market where retail is not representative, and it will return a blank, editable price rather than a guess when the evidence will not support one. Graded trading cards, fine china, fine arts, jewelry, firearms and furs are never auto-priced at all — they reach you unpriced by design.

passages.title: Documenting Clothing and Footwear in Contents Claims
passages.heading: How should clothing and footwear be documented?
passages.text: At the level the evidence supports: grouped where garments are genuinely similar and low value, itemised with brand and model where the label moves the price. A wide closet photograph supports quantity, not identity. This is the category where the gap between what a photograph proves and what a schedule claims opens the widest. Forty shirts can be forty $15 shirts or forty $200 shirts, and the difference is not visible from the doorway.

passages.title: Documenting Clothing and Footwear in Contents Claims
passages.heading: Where the value hides
passages.text: Same garment type, different property Category Low end High end Athletic shoes Generic trainers Premium or limited-release sneakers Outerwear Generic winter coat Technical shell or a down parka Shirts Multipack cotton tee Designer or technical performance garment Denim Mass-market jeans Selvedge or designer label Handbags High-street bag Designer, where line and year move the price again When the brand is visible in the evidence, it belongs on the line. When it is not, the line should say so rather than imply a tier it cannot support.

passages.title: Documenting Clothing and Footwear in Contents Claims
passages.heading: Group honestly, or itemise
passages.text: Two defensible treatments, and the one that is not Treatment When it is right When it fails Grouped line Similar quality, similar age, brand immaterial It hides six different premium labels Itemised line Brand, model or condition moves the price Forty near-identical tees as forty lines Generic catch-all Never, where evidence of brand exists It understates the wardrobe and invites a rewrite “6 generic cotton T-shirts” is a good line. “6 shirts” covering six different labels is not, and the reviewer who spots one of them in a photograph will question the rest of the schedule.

passages.title: Documenting Clothing and Footwear in Contents Claims
passages.heading: Do not let a model overstate what it saw
passages.text: A vision model looking at a closet can tell you there is a black leather shoe . It does not know the brand, the model, the material grade or the retail tier, and a schedule that fills those in anyway has invented evidence. In a densely packed closet the labels are simply not visible, and no amount of processing changes that. Kevin returns a blank, editable field rather than a confident guess when the evidence will not carry an identification. On a wardrobe that is the difference between a line you can defend and one that comes back.

passages.title: Documenting Clothing and Footwear in Contents Claims
passages.heading: Several photographs, one garment
passages.text: For anything premium, the useful set is small: the garment, and the label or style code. That is two frames, not five, and they describe one item. Kevin proposes related shots as a single item and you confirm it before anything becomes a line — which is also what keeps the item count at or below the photograph count on a claim where a closet could otherwise appear to generate more items than it has pictures.

passages.title: Documenting Clothing and Footwear in Contents Claims
passages.heading: Age carries more weight here
passages.text: Apparel and footwear classes generally carry shorter useful lives than furniture or appliances, so the age entered on a garment line moves its actual cash value further than the same number would elsewhere. A one-year-old pair of boots and a five-year-old pair are not close, and a blanket percentage across a wardrobe will be visibly wrong in both directions. Kevin classifies each line to an XactContents category and sub-category, and the class together with the age selects the rate. It is computed server-side, so a wardrobe of four hundred lines is depreciated the same way at line 400 as at line 4.

passages.title: Documenting Clothing and Footwear in Contents Claims
passages.heading: Reconstructing a wardrobe after a total loss
passages.text: When the closet is gone, quantity has to be rebuilt from what survives: photographs on phones and in the cloud, family and social photographs, order histories, card statements, retailer accounts and receipts. Those sources also tend to establish brand, which is the detail a reconstructed wardrobe most often loses. A written list can be imported and priced directly, without photographs.

passages.title: Documenting Clothing and Footwear in Contents Claims
passages.heading: Common questions
passages.text: Should every shirt be a separate line item? No, and a schedule that does it is harder to review rather than more thorough. Genuinely similar low-value garments can be grouped where quality, age and replacement basis are consistent. What should never be grouped is property that differs materially in brand or value. Can a closet photo establish all the clothing values? It can establish that clothing existed and give a rough sense of quantity. It cannot usually establish brand, product line, material or quality tier — and those are what separate a $15 shirt from a $150 one. A wide shot is context; the label is evidence. Should designer clothing be grouped with generic clothing? No, where the brand materially changes the replacement cost — which is most of the time at the premium end. Folding a designer jacket into a line of generic outerwear understates it, and the grouping is exactly what a reviewer will unpick. Does footwear depreciate differently from other contents? It can. Useful life is set by the content class rather than by the price, and apparel and footwear classes generally carry shorter lives than furniture or appliances. That is why age matters more here than almost anywhere else on the schedule. Can multiple photos be used for one clothing item? Yes, and for anything premium they should be: one frame for the garment, one for the label or the style code. Several photographs of one item become one line — never several — which is also what keeps the item count honest against the photo count. What happens when the brand is not visible? The line should say what the evidence supports and no more. Kevin returns a blank, editable field rather than a confident guess when the evidence will not carry an identification — a fabricated brand on a wardrobe line is both easy to disprove and expensive to defend.

passages.title: How to Build a 500+ Item Contents Claim
passages.heading: What makes a 500-item contents claim slow?
passages.text: Repetition, not difficulty. Identify, describe, find a replacement, check it, record the source, classify, depreciate, enter it — a few minutes an item, and a fortnight across a thousand. The answer is not to remove the review. It is to remove the repetition and spend the recovered attention on the lines that actually need a person — which is a different claim from “AI does the inventory”, and a more defensible one.

passages.title: How to Build a 500+ Item Contents Claim
passages.heading: Where the hours actually go
passages.text: Each one is minutes per item and weeks per claim Bottleneck What it costs at 500 items Organising photographs Deciding which of 1,500 frames describe the same item Identification Establishing what each item actually is Replacement research A search, several tabs and a judgment, per line Recording the source The step that gets skipped first when time is short Classification A content class on every line, consistently Depreciation Age and useful life applied the same way throughout Populating the schedule Moving all of it into the file that gets sent

passages.title: How to Build a 500+ Item Contents Claim
passages.heading: Photographs are not line items
passages.text: A 500-item claim can easily carry 1,500 to 3,000 photographs, because a careful pack-out shoots each item more than once — the item, the model plate, the damage. The first job on a large claim is therefore not pricing. It is working out which photographs belong together. Get this wrong and automation makes it worse, faster. If four photographs of one refrigerator become four refrigerators, pricing them produces four wrong lines instead of one right one — and a schedule with more items than photographs is the first thing a reviewer notices. This is why review sits before pricing rather than after it. Related frames are proposed as one item, you confirm or correct the grouping, and only then does anything become a claim line. Duplicates and context shots become no line at all.

passages.title: How to Build a 500+ Item Contents Claim
passages.heading: How it runs
passages.text: 01 Photos in Drop a folder, a phone dump or a whole .zip. Nothing is a claim line yet, and nothing is charged. 02 Reviewed Shots of one item are proposed as one item. You confirm, merge or split before anything is priced — and a line counts against your allowance once it becomes a line, not when the photo lands. 03 Priced Each line gets a price from a listing with the source kept on the row, a content class, and depreciation for its age. 04 Exported Xactimate (Excel) · .xlsx in the XactContents template, or a room-by-room PDF. An item counts against your allowance when it becomes a line, not when a photograph is uploaded — so the size of the shoot is not the size of the bill, and a photograph you exclude costs nothing.

passages.title: How to Build a 500+ Item Contents Claim
passages.heading: Scale amplifies small error rates
passages.text: Five per cent of a 20-line inventory is one line, and you will probably catch it. Five per cent of a 1,000-line inventory is fifty lines, and you will not. The comparables worth catching are the usual ones — a bundle priced as a single item, the wrong capacity, the wrong generation, an accessory standing in for the product — and every one of them is cheaper to prevent than to find later. The same logic applies to consistency. Software applies the same rule to line 900 that it applied to line 9; a person working across three weeks does not, however careful they are. On a large schedule that consistency is worth more than speed.

passages.title: How to Build a 500+ Item Contents Claim
passages.heading: Review what needs reviewing
passages.text: The goal is not to review nothing. It is to review the right lines: ambiguous identifications, unusual products, high-value property, thin pricing results, discontinued items, collectibles, and anything whose price sits far from its neighbours. Appraisal classes never price automatically at all, so they arrive on that list by default. Everything ordinary should move through with very little hand work. That is the whole trade.

passages.title: How to Build a 500+ Item Contents Claim
passages.heading: What this looked like in practice
passages.text: Kevin was built out of real public-adjuster work rather than from a product spec. In a single month, more than four thousand carrier-facing contents line items were produced through it — with a person confirming the grouping on every one of them before it became a claim item. The useful benefit is capacity rather than a stopwatch figure. Hours returned to a firm become more claims prepared, less research outsourced, and fewer weekends spent in a spreadsheet — which is a change in what the practice can take on, not just a faster file.

passages.title: How to Build a 500+ Item Contents Claim
passages.heading: Large claims still need judgment
passages.text: No large inventory runs cleanly end to end. There will be poor photographs, missing model numbers, discontinued property, collectibles and genuinely hard valuation questions. Those are the lines an experienced adjuster should be spending time on — and the reason to clear the repetitive work out of the way is to make that time available.

passages.title: How to Build a 500+ Item Contents Claim
passages.heading: Common questions
passages.text: How long should a 500-item contents claim take? There is no honest universal number — it depends on how good the photographs are, how much of the property is unusual, and how much of it needs judgment. What is predictable is where the hours go: grouping photographs, researching replacements, recording sources and applying depreciation consistently. Those are the parts worth automating. Can AI build an entire contents inventory automatically? It can remove most of the repetition, and it should not remove the review. Ambiguous identifications, high-value property, discontinued items and collectibles are exactly where an experienced adjuster is worth more than another search — and where a confident wrong answer does the most damage. Should every photo become a line item? No, and a workflow that assumes so produces a claim that is wrong in a very visible way. Several photographs routinely show one item: the item, its model plate, the damage. They are grouped into one line before anything is priced, which is why the item count on a claim is always at or below the photograph count. What is the biggest bottleneck on a large claim? Replacement-cost research, followed closely by organising the photographs and keeping depreciation consistent. Each is a few minutes on one item and a fortnight across a thousand — which is what makes them a workflow problem rather than a difficulty problem. Does a large claim cost more to run? Items are the metered dimension, not claims: Pro is $249 a month with 2,000 line items included, and claims themselves are unlimited. A line counts when it becomes a line, so excluded photographs and context shots cost nothing. Is Kevin designed for public adjusters? It was built out of one — the workflow comes from real public-adjuster practice rather than from a product spec, which is why the review step sits where it does rather than at the end.

passages.title: Contents Claim QA Checklist
passages.heading: What should be checked before a contents schedule is submitted?
passages.text: That every line identifies its item, supports its quantity, prices from something genuinely comparable with the source attached, classifies and depreciates consistently, and reconciles from the row to the total. The test for any single line is one question: could another adjuster tell what the item was, what replaces it, where the price came from and how the ACV was reached? Everything below is a way of failing that question earlier than a desk reviewer would.

passages.title: Contents Claim QA Checklist
passages.heading: 1 · The item
passages.text: Identity, quantity and the evidence behind them Check What you are looking for Description Specific enough to price — and not more specific than the evidence supports Make and model Present where a plate, badge, barcode or receipt establishes them Variant Size, capacity, generation and finish, where they move the price Quantity One item, several identical items, or a set — and the line says which Photo support Several frames of one item became one line, not several Duplicates The same property is not claimed twice, across rooms or batches In Kevin a photograph already on the claim resolves as a duplicate rather than arriving twice, and related frames are proposed as one item for you to confirm before anything becomes a line. The effect to check for is simple: the item count never exceeds the photograph count.

passages.title: Contents Claim QA Checklist
passages.heading: 2 · The price
passages.text: Where most of the argument lives Check What fails it Comparability A replacement matched on one characteristic and not the rest Bundles and sets A multi-pack pricing a single item, or the reverse Form factor Cordless priced as corded, freestanding as built-in, sectional as sofa Duplicate listings One product from nine sellers treated as nine comparables The right market Resale used where retail exists, or retail forced on a discontinued item Outliers A clearance or liquidation price standing in for replacement cost The source itself A link that no longer shows the product the line describes Open a sample of source links before you send it. Pages get updated, variant selectors reset, and listings sell out. A link that no longer supports its line is worse than no link, because it invites the reviewer to check the next one.

passages.title: Contents Claim QA Checklist
passages.heading: 3 · The arithmetic
passages.text: Reproduce one line by hand; the rest follow the same shape Check What it should do Content class Consistent with similar items elsewhere in the schedule Age How long the insured owned it, not the model year Identical ages A whole category at exactly one year old is worth a second look Depreciation Follows from class and age, the same way on every row RCV Unit cost × quantity, plus tax ACV RCV less depreciation — applied to the tax-inclusive figure Totals The schedule reconciles from the rows to the final number Depreciation in Kevin is computed server-side from the class and the age, so the worksheet and the export cannot disagree and line 400 is treated like line 4. What is worth checking is the inputs: a wrong class or a wrong age produces a perfectly consistent wrong answer.

passages.title: Contents Claim QA Checklist
passages.heading: 4 · The exceptions
passages.text: This is where review time actually belongs. The lines worth slowing down on are the ones where a small error is expensive or hard to walk back: High-value property — model, variant, configuration and condition. Collectibles — edition, condition, packaging, completeness, and which market. Discontinued items — whether the replacement path makes sense and is visible. Clothing and footwear — premium labels preserved rather than averaged into a group. Thin pricing — anything priced from very little, or not priced at all. Outliers — a price a long way from its neighbours with nothing on the row explaining it. Appraisal classes reach you unpriced by design — jewelry, firearms, fine arts, furs, fine china and graded trading cards — so they are on this list whether or not you put them there.

passages.title: Contents Claim QA Checklist
passages.heading: 5 · The file
passages.text: Before the export leaves Check Why Line numbers Stable — an export already sent cites them, so they are never renumbered Room and location Correct, and the same property is not sitting in two rooms Incomplete lines Listed as exceptions rather than quietly filled in The right claim Right claim, right insured, right format Format Xactimate (Excel) .xlsx in the XactContents template, or the PDF Kevin never blocks an export on any of this. The dialog tells you what needs attention and the download stays live, because whether to send it is your call rather than the software’s.

passages.title: Contents Claim QA Checklist
passages.heading: The one-line test
passages.text: If you only do one pass, do this one: pick ten lines at random and ask whether a stranger could follow each from the item to the ACV without asking you a question. The schedule is as strong as the weakest line somebody happens to open.

passages.title: Contents Claim QA Checklist
passages.heading: Common questions
passages.text: What is a contents claim QA review? A pass over the finished schedule before it leaves your hands, checking that each line identifies its item, supports its quantity, prices from something comparable, depreciates consistently and reconciles arithmetically. It is cheaper than answering the same questions one at a time after a desk review. Should every line be checked to the same depth? No, and a schedule of several hundred lines makes that impossible anyway. Routine property can be scanned; high-value, unusual, discontinued and collectible lines are where a few minutes each is worth spending, because that is where an error is expensive. What are the most common contents inventory mistakes? Vague descriptions, duplicated items, replacements that are not really comparable, prices with no source, depreciation applied inconsistently, and quantity errors. Most of them scale with the size of the claim rather than appearing once. Does Kevin check any of this automatically? Some of it is prevented rather than checked: a photograph already on the claim resolves as a duplicate, related frames are proposed as one item before anything becomes a line, depreciation is computed server-side from class and age so it cannot drift between rows, and a line Kevin cannot price arrives blank rather than guessed. The judgment calls are still yours. How do I check the arithmetic quickly? Take one line and reproduce it by hand: unit cost × quantity, plus tax, less depreciation, equals ACV. Depreciation applies to the tax-inclusive figure, so a line that foots any other way is worth understanding before the whole schedule inherits it. What should I do about lines that are still incomplete? Leave them visible rather than filling them in. An explicit exception list — missing age, missing model, needs a better photograph, needs a source — is far easier to defend than a schedule that looks complete because the gaps were papered over.

passages.title: Why Contents Line Items Get Questioned
passages.heading: Why do contents line items get questioned or reduced?
passages.text: Because the line does not carry its own argument: the description is too vague to price, the replacement is not comparable, the quantity is unsupported, the price has no source, or the depreciation does not match similar lines. Nearly all of these are preventable in the five minutes before a schedule is sent, and expensive in the weeks after. Grouped below by what is actually wrong, because the fix differs: an identity problem needs evidence, a pricing problem needs a better comparable, and a consistency problem needs the whole schedule looked at rather than the one row.

passages.title: Why Contents Line Items Get Questioned
passages.heading: Identity problems
passages.text: The line does not establish what the property was Problem What the reviewer sees The fix Description too vague “Television — $2,100”, with no way to judge it Brand, size, technology, tier Model unsupported Specificity nothing in the file backs Cite the plate, receipt or record — or drop it Quantity unsupported Quantity 18 against evidence for a few Document or reconstruct the count Duplicates The same property on two lines or in two rooms Group the photographs before promoting Invented specificity is its own failure mode. A model number nothing supports looks stronger than a generic description right up until somebody checks it, and then it costs more than the vagueness would have. This is why Kevin returns a blank, editable field rather than a confident guess.

passages.title: Why Contents Line Items Get Questioned
passages.heading: Comparable problems
passages.text: The replacement is not the same property Problem Example Not actually comparable Matched on size while tier, technology or capacity differ A bundle pricing one item One cordless drill priced from a five-piece kit Wrong variant Wrong capacity, generation, battery platform or model suffix Wrong form factor Corded for cordless, built-in for freestanding, sofa for sectional Source does not match the line The page changed, or the variant selector reset Outlier pricing Clearance, liquidation, or a specialty bundle standing in for retail Weak discontinued logic An unrelated modern product chosen because it was available The pattern underneath all of these is the same: one characteristic was matched and treated as if it were all of them. That is the subject of exact match vs like kind and quality .

passages.title: Why Contents Line Items Get Questioned
passages.heading: Consistency problems
passages.text: These are the ones that cannot be fixed one row at a time, because the row is not really the problem — the schedule is. Two similar items at the same age depreciating differently, with nothing explaining it. One blanket percentage applied across categories with very different useful lives. Ages missing, or an entire category sharing one round number. Descriptions that get thinner as the schedule goes on. A line with no source at all, in a schedule where most lines have one. Depreciation in Kevin is computed server-side from the content class and the age, so two similar rows cannot drift apart through repetition — and the worksheet and the export cannot disagree about a figure. The inputs are still yours to get right.

passages.title: Why Contents Line Items Get Questioned
passages.heading: Questioned does not mean denied
passages.text: A reviewer asking about a line is usually asking for something specific: a better description, a better comparable, support for a quantity, a model or an age clarified. Lines get removed when they cannot be answered, not when they are challenged. Which is the practical argument for keeping the source on the row rather than in a folder. The question arrives months later, and the difference between answering it and rebuilding the research is whether the evidence travelled with the line.

passages.title: Why Contents Line Items Get Questioned
passages.heading: A line that survives review
passages.text: It answers five things without anyone asking: what is it, how do we know, what replaces it, what does that replacement cost, and how was the depreciation calculated. Everything on this page is a way of failing one of those five.

passages.title: Why Contents Line Items Get Questioned
passages.heading: Common questions
passages.text: Why do contents line items get reduced? Most often because the line does not support the number rather than because the property did not exist: a vague description, a replacement that is not really comparable, a quantity nothing backs, a price with no source, or depreciation that does not match similar lines. Can a line be questioned even with a source link? Yes, and this is the most common surprise. A link to the wrong product is not evidence — it is a faster way to find the error. The comparable behind the URL still has to be the same property at the same tier and quantity. Is a higher-priced replacement automatically wrong? No. If the only current product that matches the original’s quality costs more than the original did, that is the replacement cost. What draws scrutiny is a higher price with nothing on the line explaining why that product is the comparable. Should a questioned line be removed? Usually not. The reviewer is normally asking for something — a clarified model, a better comparable, support for a quantity — and the right response is to answer it. Removing a line concedes property the insured owned. What is the single most common avoidable error? Quantity, on bundles and sets. A multi-pack pricing one item inflates the line by the multiple, and a single unit pricing a set understates it. Both are easy to spot in review and easy to prevent before sending. How does Kevin reduce these? In the places it honestly can: a photograph already on the claim resolves as a duplicate rather than becoming a second line, related frames are proposed as one item before anything is promoted, depreciation is computed server-side from class and age so two similar rows cannot drift apart, and an item it cannot price confidently arrives blank and editable rather than guessed.

passages.title: How to Document Source Pricing for Contents Claims
passages.heading: What makes a replacement-cost source defensible?
passages.text: That it leads to the specific product used for the price, at the right quantity, from a seller appropriate to the item — and that the relationship between that product and the damaged one is visible on the line. The failure this prevents is not a missing URL. It is a URL that opens on something other than what the line describes, which is worse than no source at all: it gives a reviewer a reason to check the next one.

passages.title: How to Document Source Pricing for Contents Claims
passages.heading: What a source has to establish
passages.text: A link is the delivery mechanism, not the evidence Element Why it matters The specific product A direct product page, not a search result or a category Manufacturer and model So the comparable can be checked against the item Variant Size, capacity, generation and finish, where they move the price Quantity basis One chair or a set of four; one battery or a two-pack Seller Whether it is the retailer or a third-party marketplace listing Price The figure the line actually used Relationship to the item Exact, successor, same-brand or like-kind — and why

passages.title: How to Document Source Pricing for Contents Claims
passages.heading: Match the source to the property
passages.text: Different sources answer different questions Source Good for Watch for Major retailer Current consumer property still sold new Third-party sellers on the same domain Manufacturer Successor models and specifications List price that nobody actually charges Specialist retailer Niche or professional equipment Thin availability Resale marketplace Discontinued, vintage and collectible property Condition, completeness and edition A listing on a major retailer’s domain is not automatically a retail price. Large sites carry third-party marketplace sellers whose pricing can be well above or below ordinary retail, and the badge saying so is easy to miss. Check who is actually selling it.

passages.title: How to Document Source Pricing for Contents Claims
passages.heading: Quantity is the quiet error
passages.text: A source price has to represent the same quantity the line claims. One chair against a set of four, one drill against a five-piece kit, one plate against a twelve-piece service, one battery against a two-pack — each inflates or deflates the line by a clean multiple, which makes it both easy to spot in review and easy to miss while building.

passages.title: How to Document Source Pricing for Contents Claims
passages.heading: Prices move, and that is fine
passages.text: Replacement cost is what the item costs to replace now , so a product that goes on sale, sells out or is superseded changes the figure. A source documents the price it supported at the time it was used; treating it as a permanent historical fact is how a schedule ends up defending a number nobody can reproduce. On a claim that runs for months the practical consequence is that lines sometimes need re-pricing — which is quick when the listing is on the row and slow when it is not.

passages.title: How to Document Source Pricing for Contents Claims
passages.heading: Discontinued and collectible property
passages.text: When the exact item is gone, the source has a second job: making the replacement path visible. A successor model from the manufacturer, or a comparable from the resale market where retail no longer represents the item, should be identifiable as that from the line rather than looking like an arbitrary substitution. For a collectible, a single asking price is rarely the whole picture — edition, condition, packaging and completeness all move the value, and the comparable has to match on those before its price means anything.

passages.title: How to Document Source Pricing for Contents Claims
passages.heading: How Kevin keeps it
passages.text: Each engine-priced line is priced from a single listing rather than a blend of several, and that listing is stored on the row and printed into the export — so the chain runs from the damaged item to the identified property to the replacement, its source and the price, and then to RCV and ACV. A price you enter by hand carries your own source link instead, attached the same way.

passages.title: How to Document Source Pricing for Contents Claims
passages.heading: Common questions
passages.text: Is a source required for every item? Requirements vary by carrier and by claim, so there is no universal rule. What is consistent is that a price with its listing attached is far easier to evaluate — and that the question "where did this come from" is the one that arrives most often, usually months later. Is a screenshot better than a link? They do different jobs. A screenshot preserves what was visible on a date; a link shows what the product costs now. For a claim that may run for months, having the link means the line can be re-priced rather than re-researched — which is why Kevin stores the link and the figure together. Should the source always be a major retailer? No. The source should fit the item: a major retailer for current consumer property, a manufacturer for a successor model or a specification, a specialist for niche equipment, and the resale market for discontinued, vintage or collectible property that ordinary retail no longer represents. Can a source price change during the claim? Yes, and that is normal rather than a problem. Replacement cost is what the item costs to replace now, so a product that goes on sale or increases in price moves the figure. A source documents the price it supported when it was used; it is not a permanent fact. What makes a source weak even when the link works? The product behind it. Wrong model, wrong size or capacity, a set where one item is claimed, a used listing where a new replacement is being priced, or a third-party seller whose price is not representative. The URL is the least important part of a source. Does Kevin keep the source? Yes. Each engine-priced line is priced from a single listing rather than a blend of several, and that listing is stored on the row and printed into the export. A price you type in yourself carries your own source link instead.

passages.title: Useful Life by Content Class
passages.heading: Common questions
passages.text: What is useful life in a contents claim? The number of years a class of property is expected to last, which is what a straight-line schedule divides an item’s age by. A six-year-old refrigerator against a fourteen-year life is 43% depreciated; the same age against a three-year life is fully depreciated. Why do two similar items depreciate differently? Because the class decides the life, not the price or the look of the item. Footwear, furniture and major appliances have very different expected lives, which is exactly why a single blanket percentage across a schedule comes apart under review. Does depreciation really run to 100%? Yes. Property past its useful life shows an actual cash value of $0.00 rather than stopping at a floor we invented. Only one line in the whole schedule carries a cap, and the reference above marks it. Which classes are never priced automatically? Six of them, marked in the table: jewelry, firearms, fine arts, furs, fine china and graded trading cards. They reach you unpriced with an editable field, because a number produced without an appraisal on that property is worse than a blank. Why do some lines have no useful life at all? Because age is not what drives their value. Those lines depreciate on a different basis — a flat rate, a percentage of replacement cost, or not at all — rather than on a years-owned calculation. The table says which applies to each. Is this the schedule Kevin actually applies? Yes, and that is the point of publishing it. passages.title: Photo-Based vs Description-Only Contents Pricing
passages.heading: Which is better, pricing from photographs or from descriptions?
passages.text: Photographs, wherever usable ones exist — they establish which product it was rather than which product it resembled. Descriptions are the right route when the property and its photographs are both gone. The two are often presented as a preference. They are not. A description records what somebody remembers; a photograph of a model plate records what the item was. On property where the model moves the price, that is the whole valuation — and no amount of careful writing closes the gap.

passages.heading: What each route can establish
passages.text: Same item, two kinds of evidence From photographs From a description The item exists Shown Asserted Brand Read off the badge or plate Only if the writer knew it Model Read off the label or barcode Only if the writer knew it Variant Capacity, size and finish are visible Only if stated Condition Visible, and the damage with it Reported Quantity Countable in frame Reconstructed Grouping Several shots become one line Not applicable — a row is a line A written line may say 65-inch Samsung TV . A photograph of the label says QN65S90D OLED . Those price differently, and only one of them can be checked by somebody who was not there.

passages.title: Photo-Based vs Description-Only Contents Pricing
passages.heading: When description-only is the right route
passages.text: A total fire loss where the contents and any photographs of them are gone. Property removed or disposed of before anyone documented it. A restoration company’s or mover’s inventory that exists only as a PDF. An insured rebuilding a list from memory, receipts and purchase histories. In each of those, waiting for photographic evidence is not an option, and a written inventory is the best remaining one. What it is not is a shortcut on a claim where the property is still there to photograph.

passages.title: Photo-Based vs Description-Only Contents Pricing
passages.heading: A total loss does not mean no evidence
passages.text: The property is gone; the record of it often is not. Before a list is built from memory alone, it is worth pulling what survives elsewhere — because each of these can supply the brand or model a description would otherwise guess at: Photographs on phones and in cloud backups, including family and social photographs. Retailer account order histories, which carry exact models and dates. Email receipts, card statements, warranty records and manuals. Old listings or insurance schedules from a previous policy.

passages.title: Photo-Based vs Description-Only Contents Pricing
passages.heading: Common questions
passages.text: Can you build a contents claim without photos? Yes. Total-loss inventories are routinely reconstructed from a typed list, a restoration company’s inventory, receipts and purchase records. Each described row is researched and priced like a photographed item would be — what you lose is the brand and model precision that only evidence can supply. Are photo-based inventories more accurate? Usually, and for one specific reason: a photograph of a model plate establishes which product it was, while a description establishes what somebody remembers it was. On property where the model moves the price, that gap is the whole valuation. Should description-only pricing be used when photos exist? No. If usable item-level photographs exist, they are stronger evidence and they are already in hand. The written route exists because total losses are real, not because it is an easier option. What makes a written description good enough to price? Brand, model or collection, size or capacity, quality tier, age and quantity — roughly in that order of value. “Sofa” prices as a generic sofa. “Pottery Barn Andes sectional, 3-seat, 6 years old” prices as that, and the difference is not small. Does a written list go through the same review as photos? No, and it does not need to. Review exists to turn several photographs into one item; a written row already is a line item, so it goes straight to the worksheet. The mapping and preview steps replace it, and neither creates anything until you import. What if some items have photos and some do not? Use both. Photograph what survives, import the rest as a written list, and they land in the same worksheet and export the same way. Nothing forces a claim down one route.

passages.title: What Is Insurance-Grade Contents Documentation?
passages.heading: What makes contents documentation insurance-grade?
passages.text: That a line answers four questions on its own: what the item was, what replaces it, where the replacement price came from, and how the actual cash value was reached — with the evidence attached rather than remembered. The distinction that matters is between recognising an object and valuing a specific piece of property. A system can be entirely right that it is looking at a television and still have established nothing a claim can use.

passages.title: What Is Insurance-Grade Contents Documentation?
passages.heading: Two different problems
passages.text: Why a correct detection is not a documented line Object detection Insurance documentation Answers What kind of thing is visible What this specific property was Output A category An identified item with a price and a basis Evidence The frame itself The frame, the label, the listing, the schedule Good enough for Triage, quantity, a rough list A figure somebody else has to accept

passages.title: What Is Insurance-Grade Contents Documentation?
passages.heading: What a documented line carries
passages.text: Eight parts, in the order they depend on each other Part What it has to do Identity As specific as the evidence supports — and no more Evidence Photographs, labels, receipts or records the line traces back to Quantity One item, several, or a set — stated, not inferred from a crowded frame Replacement Matching on function, quality, specification and tier Source The listing the price came from, kept on the row Classification A content class, which decides the useful life Depreciation Age against that life, applied the same way throughout Traceability The whole chain readable from the row Read end to end that is one sentence: evidence → identified item → replacement → source → RCV → depreciation → ACV . A line that breaks anywhere along it is the line that comes back.

passages.title: What Is Insurance-Grade Contents Documentation?
passages.heading: Proportional detail, not maximum detail
passages.text: Insurance-grade does not mean every item carries a model number. It means the identification matches what moves the price. A premium camera body needs its model, configuration and lens; a bath towel needs to be a bath towel. Inventing specificity on the second is not thoroughness — it is the detail a reviewer checks first and the fastest way to make a schedule look unreliable. A professional inventory does not hide uncertainty. Where the evidence will not carry an identification, the honest line says so: Kevin returns a blank, editable field rather than a plausible guess, because a confident wrong description survives review and a blank does not.

passages.title: What Is Insurance-Grade Contents Documentation?
passages.heading: Where room-level detection falls short
passages.text: A room photograph is useful for context and rough quantity. It is weak for valuation because the things that set value are the things it cannot resolve: labels, tags, model numbers, materials, edition details, condition and tier. A closet photograph might show thirty shirts. It will not show which are designer, which are technical apparel and which came in a multipack — and pricing all thirty as average-grade clothing produces a number quickly without producing a defensible one. That is also why several photographs of one item have to become one line rather than several: a schedule reporting more items than photographs is wrong in a way a reviewer spots immediately.

passages.title: What Is Insurance-Grade Contents Documentation?
passages.heading: The test
passages.text: Pick any line at random and hand it to somebody who was not there. If they can tell what the item was, what replaces it, where the price came from and how the ACV was reached — without asking you a question — the line is insurance-grade. If they cannot, no amount of volume elsewhere in the schedule fixes it.

passages.title: What Is Insurance-Grade Contents Documentation?
passages.heading: Common questions
passages.text: What makes a contents inventory insurance-grade? That another claims professional can read a line and answer four questions without asking you: what the item was, what replaces it, where the price came from, and how the actual cash value was reached. Everything else is a means to that. Is object detection enough for an insurance claim? Rarely on its own. Detection answers what KIND of thing is visible; valuation needs which specific product it was. “Television” and “Samsung 65-inch OLED, S90D” are the same detection result and very different claims. Does every item need a model number? No, and insisting on it produces invented detail. The level of identification should match what moves the price: a premium camera needs its model, a bath towel does not. Proportional detail is the standard, not maximum detail. Why are source links important? Because a price without its listing is an assertion and a price with one is evidence. The question that comes back most often is where a figure came from, and a line that already answers it never generates that round trip. Can AI produce insurance-grade documentation? It can produce most of it and should not be trusted with all of it. The repetition — research, sourcing, classification, depreciation — is exactly what software is for. Ambiguous identifications, high-value property and collectibles are where a person is worth more than another search. What should a line do when the evidence is thin? Say so. A blank, editable field is stronger documentation than a confident guess, because the guess survives review and the blank does not. Hiding uncertainty is the one failure that gets worse with time.

passages.text: A demo that turns one room photograph into hundreds of items is genuinely impressive, and for triage — what was in here, roughly how much of it — it is useful. The question to carry into the trial is what each of those lines can support once a desk reviewer opens it. The more an item’s value rests on brand, model, material, edition or quality tier, the more item-level evidence it takes to price. A closet photograph establishes that thirty shirts existed; it does not establish which three were designer, and pricing all thirty as mid-range produces a figure quickly without producing a defensible one. Speed and accuracy are not opposites, but they are not the same measurement, and only one of them is visible in a demo. One arithmetic check settles a lot of it: does the tool ever report more items than you took photographs? On a contents claim some frames are context, some are a second angle of something already counted, and some are unreadable — so the honest item count is at or below the photo count. A number above it has to come from somewhere.

passages.text: Where does the 4,000 figure come from? From Kevin’s own founder, who is a practising adjuster: 4,000+ carrier-facing contents line items produced through Kevin on his claims during a single month. It is a first-party figure from the person who ran the work, not an audited third-party study, and we would rather say that plainly than dress it up. Does that mean 4,000 items were created without review? No. Every line passed through the same review step everyone else gets: grouping confirmed before promotion, identifications corrected where wrong, and blank prices filled in by hand. Volume came from removing the typing, not from removing the person. What was still done by hand? Grouping decisions on ambiguous sets, identifications the evidence did not support, unusual comparables, and the claim-specific judgment calls — which items are a total loss, what the insured can document, what a particular desk will question. Does this mean Kevin will do the same on my claims? It means the volume is achievable with one adjuster and this workflow. Your mix matters: a claim of mostly branded, photographable property automates further than one full of custom or collectible items, which need a person either way. Why is there no hours-saved number on this page? Because the figures we currently publish elsewhere do not agree with each other, and we are not going to settle that disagreement by picking the flattering one. When the per-claim arithmetic is reconciled it will appear here with its basis stated.

passages.heading: Common questions
passages.text: What is considered contents for insurance purposes? Broadly, the things that would fall out if you turned the house upside down — furniture, appliances that are not built in, electronics, clothing, kitchenware, tools, décor, toys and linens. What is attached to the building is usually structure, not contents. Jewelry, firearms, fine art and furs are contents but most policies cap them separately, so list them and let the adjuster apply the limit. What is the best way to create an inventory list? Room by room, one row per item, with a photograph of anything whose brand or model affects the price. Work through one room completely before moving on — it is far easier to remember what was on a shelf while you are picturing that shelf than to list the whole house by category. How detailed does the description need to be? Detailed enough that someone who never saw the item could shop for it. Size, material, colour, capacity and the number of pieces all change the price. "Rug" could be $40 or $4,000; "8x10 wool area rug, hand-knotted, blue" could not. What if I do not know the brand or model? Leave those cells empty. A blank is honest and gets priced from the description; a guessed brand sends the search after the wrong product and the error survives into the claim. If you find a receipt later, add it then. Do I need photographs as well as the list? They help, and for anything where brand or model moves the price they help a lot — a photograph of a model plate settles a question a description cannot. But the list works on its own, which is the point of it for a total loss where nothing survived to photograph. What happens after I send this to my adjuster? passages.text: It isn’t an appraisal. Kevin prices from live retail comps and shows you the listing each number came from. It doesn’t decide anything. Special limits are flagged, never enforced. Every price, content class, age and depreciation percentage on the worksheet is yours to overrule, and the audit log records that you did. It won’t hold your work hostage. No readiness gate on an export, no approval step, no “not ready yet”. Kevin surfaces what deserves a second look — unpriced lines, missing model numbers, capped classes — and then gets out of the way. It isn’t a compliance system. Retention and record-keeping obligations belong to you and the carrier, not to us. Kevin keeps everything and never deletes to reclaim space, but it does not pretend to be your system of record. passages.heading: Every step, start to export.
passages.text: Written walkthrough Every step, start to export. Exactly what you do on a real contents loss — a folder of photos in, a priced line-item inventory out, about 20 minutes of your time. 01 Start the claim ~1 min Enter the claim number, policy number, date and cause of loss. Pick the carrier and the insured; type the loss address — the ZIP auto-resolves the sales-tax rate that lands in every line. Choose the contents coverage label off the declarations page (Coverage C, Personal Property, Contents…) and enter the limit, so Kevin warns you as the inventory approaches it. 02 Drop the photos ~2 min for hundreds of photos Drag in a folder, a phone dump, or a whole .zip — no total-size cap, up to 15 MB per photo. Duplicates are hashed out on arrival. Kevin pre-groups shots taken seconds apart into photo sets, so three angles of one sofa become one line item, not three. Review the proposed sets: merge two that belong together, split one that does not, exclude context shots, and optionally add a note — additional identification for Kevin ("the TV is the Sony, not the Samsung"). 03 Let Kevin work ~8 min, unattended Each set is identified — item, make, model number off the plate or barcode where it is readable. Kevin assigns a content class, then pulls retail comps per item and prices it from one of them — an actual listing, which the Source Link points at. Depreciation comes from the schedule on the claim — straight-line by default — and ACV is derived from it. Anything Kevin cannot price confidently arrives blank instead of guessed. 04 Review the worksheet 20–40 min for a few hundred lines One grid, every cell editable: room, quantity, description, make, model, class, unit cost, age and depreciation. Click a row number to open the item panel — source photo, the three comps with dated proof links, and the depreciation math. Pin it to keep it beside the grid as you work down the list. Fix a bad identification by editing the description and re-pricing against fresh comps; type a price for anything left blank. Filter by room, group by class, and check the special-limits flags. 05 Export and send ~1 min Xactimate-ready .xlsx on the XactContents template — column parity, so it imports without cleanup. Or a client-facing PDF inventory, or the full bundle: spreadsheet, PDF, every photo, and the audit log. Download it or mint an expiring share link. Ask us anything specific — kevin@kevin.co — and we’ll answer with the actual practice, not a badge.
